title: The Sacred Heart
hook: a Friday feast: the heart of Christ as love made visible
tomorrow: The Birth of John the Baptist (24 June)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Corpus Christi, the host carried through town. Your line was carried through the streets. Who on your street did you carry? Day six hundred seventy-three.

It's in your grandmother's kitchen, maybe, or above the door of an Irish farmhouse, or on a holy card in a wallet. Jesus, looking straight out, pointing to his own chest, where a heart is shown outside his robe: wrapped in thorns, topped with flames and a small cross, sometimes with a wound in its side. It can look strange to anyone who didn't grow up with it. A heart on fire, on the outside of a body. But for millions of Catholic homes it's the most familiar picture in the house. On a Friday in June, the Church keeps its feast.
screen: `A PICTURE IN THE KITCHEN.` → `A HEART ON FIRE, OUTSIDE.` → `A FRIDAY IN JUNE.`

segments.voice: The heart in that picture starts in John's Gospel, at the cross, in the Douay-Rheims: "But one of the soldiers with a spear opened his side, and immediately there came out blood and water." Early Christian writers saw in that open side the birth of the Church, its sacraments flowing out. Medieval saints, women and men, wrote about resting in the wounded heart of Christ. Then, in the 1670s, in a convent at Paray-le-Monial in France, a nun named Margaret Mary Alacoque reported a series of visions. In them, Jesus showed her his heart and complained, in her telling, that it had loved people so much and was repaid with coldness. Behold this heart, he said. He asked for a feast on the Friday after the octave of Corpus Christi, and for people to receive communion on the first Friday of each month. Her claims met real resistance at first. It took almost two centuries before Pope Pius IX, in 1856, put the feast on the calendar for the whole Church. Now it falls on the Friday after the second Sunday after Pentecost, which usually lands in June, and June became the month of the Sacred Heart. What's the picture saying? That God's love isn't an idea. It has a body, a pulse, and wounds. Jesus describes his own heart once in the Gospels, and he doesn't say mighty. He says, "learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart."
screen: `A SPEAR OPENS HIS SIDE.` · `MARGARET MARY, 1670S.` · `PIUS IX, 1856: THE WHOLE CHURCH.` · `LOVE WITH A PULSE AND WOUNDS.` · then, large: `I AM MEEK, AND HUMBLE OF HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: your hand on your heart. Sit, and place one hand flat on your chest. Wait until you can feel the beat. Count a few. That rhythm has been going since before you were born, without your help. Then think of one person you love who is hard to love right now. Keep your hand there. If you pray, you can pray for them, or simply say Jesus's line, meek and humble of heart. If you don't, feel the beat and wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Sacred Heart. The heart of Jesus, honored as love made visible, wounded and burning. Its feast is a Friday in June, for the whole Church since 1856. Today's word.
Your line: behold this heart. Today, when someone is cold to you, put a hand on your chest for one beat before you answer. Day six hundred seventy-three.

screen: `DAY 673 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BIRTH OF JOHN THE BAPTIST (24 JUNE).`

howItsDone: Catholics keep the solemnity of the Sacred Heart on the Friday after the second Sunday after Pentecost, usually in June; many homes display a Sacred Heart image, and some Catholics practice the First Friday devotion of receiving communion on the first Friday of each month.

original.note: Latin: the heart of Jesus, from the feast's name, Sacratissimum Cor Iesu.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old-fashioned picture in grandma's kitchen.
what it means: Christ's love shown with a body: a heart wounded, crowned with thorns, burning.
what a scholar hears: John 19:34's open side read as the Church's birth, Margaret Mary's visions in the 1670s, and Pius IX's extension in 1856.

notes: Margaret Mary's 'great apparition' (1675) asked for the feast on the Friday after the octave of Corpus Christi; confirm.
Pius IX extended the feast to the universal Church in 1856; confirm.
The claim that the Gospel's only self-description of Jesus's heart is Matthew 11:29 (as phrased in the myth) is worded carefully; confirm it's fair.
'Behold this heart' is the traditional English summary of her account; paraphrased, not quoted.
Patristic reading of John 19:34 as the birth of the Church and sacraments (e.g. Augustine, Chrysostom); confirm.
